title: Prince Robinson
summary: Budd praises Prince Robinson as nearly equal to Hawkins and recalls Clyde Hart copying his solo on 'Zonky'.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: So -- okay, excuse me. But how about Prince Robertson? That's another great --

Oh, Prince Robertson, man! Prince Robertson, now he was running Coleman Hawkins a tight fight, because the cats were debating -- when I first heard of Prince Robertson was McKinney Cottonpickers-- I said, who is th is cat? Because he was sounding as great as Coleman Hawkins to me, almost, because actually Hawk was my inspiration. And Prince Robertson, man, was running Hawk a close second. And he played with the McKinney's Cottonpickers, and this -- was from New Orleans Prince with some darlings -- and played an awful, terrific amount of clarinet and one of the finest gentlemen that I have

ever met. And I'm sure if he were living today he would still be a threat to all clarinet and tenor players. He had a unique style. I never will forget when Clyde Hart, as I told you before, was copying the records of the Japain music. He copied a solo of Prince Robinson's that Ben Webster had to play, see?
And I never will forget the the break -- the thing was on Zonky. A thing called 'Zonky'.

You know, Zonky, say, Da-da-da-dee-da-da-da-da-a-a -- Don Redmond's arrange -- da-de-da-da-a-a-- it brings me to play -- zhi-doo-doo-doo-doodle-doo-deedle-daw, you know? And I say, God dog, you know, like because back in those days, slap tonguing was still just like, you know, slapping the bass.

And if you really couldn't do a few slap tonguing licks, I mean then you really wasn't too hot, you know. And Prince, he had that roughest and that goodest sound, like a Hawk, and we all started to be changing to Prince Robertson, and we tried to find everything that he ever recorded.
